newsitem.title: USA: White House gives way to Republicans on documents.
newsitem.headline: White House gives way to Republicans on documents.

text.p: The White House gave way to Republican pressure on Tuesday by agreeing to hand over thousands of pages of documents relating to campaign fund raising, averting a looming legal showdown.

Facing the threat of "contempt of Congress" criminal proceedings this week, White House counsel Charles Ruff agreed to deliver on Tuesday some 2,000 pages of documents to the House government reform and oversight committee, which is investigating alleged illegal or improper fund raising in the 1996 elections.
In a letter to Indiana Representative Dan Burton, the Republican committee chairman, Ruff made several promises, starting with a commitment to deliver the 2,000 pages immediately.
He also promised to provide uncensored copies of previously censored documents and to supply a detailed list of a small number of documents the White House was still refusing to hand over by June 13.

Burton hailed the concession as a major success. "This is a victory for the people's right to know. We gave up nothing. We said we were going to be persistent and consistent with our demands until we got every document we need," he said.

The committee is investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.

It is also investigating whether the White House or the Democrats knowingly solicited, received or laundered foreign funds. The FBI and a Senate committee are conducting simultaneous but separate investigations.
Ruff had previously said he would allow Burton and committee investigators to view copies of certain documents at the White House but not to copy or remove them for fear they may be leaked.
He is still refusing to hand over some 40 documents, which he has argued are subject to attorney-client privilege.
Burton said he reserved the right to take action to secure those documents as well if he thought they were necessary for his investigation.
He also said he would make any document public if he determined it contained information that the American people ought to know.

Some of the documents relate to former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, who was recently released after serving an 18-month jail sentence for defrauding his Arkansas law firm. He worked there alongside first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.
In the period between resigning from the Justice Department and beginning his sentence, Hubbell received more than $500,000 from various individuals and companies for work as a legal consultant.
Burton suspects it was hush money to prevent Hubbell from testifying about what he knew. Hubbell indicated he will invoke the Fifth Amendment and refuse to testify further.

Other documents demanded by the committee related to the activities of Asian-Americans and Asian business interests, including former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang. Burton has said he suspects Huang was a spy working for China.
